title: Build an NDA triage system
description: A system that sorts incoming NDAs into auto-approve, minor edits, or attorney review before anyone reads the whole document.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

triage.title: Triage
triage.content: Sorting items by urgency or importance to decide what gets attention first. Your email-manager skill triages your inbox — it separates messages that need a real reply from noise you can ignore.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

workflow.title: Workflow
workflow.content: A multi-step process Claude runs to accomplish a goal — for example: read emails → filter by topic → summarize → post to Slack. Workflows can be run manually or on a schedule.

anthropic.title: Anthropic
anthropic.content: The company that created Claude. An AI safety company focused on building reliable, interpretable AI systems.

routing-pattern.title: Routing (Orchestration Pattern)
routing-pattern.content: An orchestration pattern where a classifier looks at the input and sends it down a specialized path — support tickets to the refund flow, bug reports to the triage flow. Each path stays simple because it only handles its own kind of input.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Most incoming NDAs are boilerplate, but each one still lands on a lawyer's desk for a full read. [Anthropic](#tooltip-anthropic)'s own [Claude Legal plugin](https://claude.com/plugins/legal) ships a dedicated NDA-[triage](#tooltip-triage) command, described as rapid NDA pre-screening that sorts incoming NDAs into standard approval, counsel review, or full review, confirming this three-tier pattern is a supported [workflow](#tooltip-workflow).

Even mature legal AI deployments still route a meaningful share of repetitive compliance and contract work to a human, a fair baseline for how much NDA volume this system can realistically absorb. This system classifies each incoming NDA as standard, minor edits needed, or attorney review required, with a stated reason for the call, so counsel spends time on the ones that need it.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) each time an NDA lands, a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill), or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) tied to your intake portal or e-signature tool. Every version needs a written standard to compare against before it can classify anything.
Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your standard NDA template, your tier rules, your intake source, and your notification path.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that triages incoming NDAs into standard, needs-minor-edits, or needs-attorney-review, with a reason for each call. Ask me questions, one at a time, about what counts as a standard NDA for us, what edits are minor enough to auto-flag versus what needs a lawyer, how NDAs arrive today, and who gets notified for each tier. When you have what you need, write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to define "standard" in writing before the system has to guess, and the scope document becomes the brief for every build session after it.

items: Where NDAs enter your workflow today, since the intake point decides how this plugs in.
What counts as a minor edit in your organization, since that line is where most of the time savings live.
Who gets notified for each tier and how fast, since a standard NDA sitting unsigned defeats the point.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common connectors are your inbox or intake portal (Gmail, Typeform) where NDAs arrive, e-signature tools (DocuSign, HelloSign) for standard approvals, and your document management system for logging every triage decision. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real NDA. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Classify the attached NDA as standard, minor edits needed, or attorney review required, with a specific reason for the classification.

Context: Our standard NDA template and acceptable variations are documented in [location]. NDAs typically arrive from [source, e.g. an inbox, a portal, a Slack channel]. Past triage decisions are logged in [location] for consistency reference.

Rules:
- Compare against our own standard template and named acceptable variations, not a generic idea of what an NDA should say.
- Classify as "standard" only if every clause matches an approved position exactly.
- Classify as "minor edits" only for deviations on a named list of low-risk clauses (e.g. notice period, governing law within an approved set).
- Anything outside those two categories is "attorney review," with the specific clause and reason stated.
- Never auto-approve based on the counterparty's reputation or deal size; classify the document on its terms alone.
Output format: classification, reason, and the specific clause(s) driving the call.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: naming the exact clauses that separate the tiers makes "standard" auditable.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Right tier, specific clause cited, no shortcut on reputation or deal size?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong and fold the correction into the rules.

items: Keep a running log of triage decisions so patterns in counterparty pushback become visible.
Extend the pattern to other high-volume, low-variance documents like order forms or standard MSAs.
Run a quarterly review of "minor edit" calls to confirm the category boundary still holds.
Add an auto-send step for standard NDAs by connecting your e-signature tool through a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors) once trust in the classification is established.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft rubric and run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each NDA classification, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, NDA classified, tier assigned, whether the tier held up on review, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make a drifting tier boundary visible after a few weeks of entries.

children.text: **Log** every run. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an unwritten instruction.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes weeks straight, package the prompt and corrected rules into a skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. Silent scope creep in what counts as standard, where an edge case gets auto-approved because it resembled one on the surface. Review a sample of auto-approved documents on a schedule.
